topic: Station restrictions, RACES, space and telecommand stations

notes.front: What is the radiolocation service to an amateur transmitting on 70 cm?
notes.back: A service whose United States Government stations 70 cm amateurs must not interfere with, and whose interference they must accept.
notes.explanation: Section 97.303(b) puts the same duty on the 33 cm, 23 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm bands and the 24.05–24.25 GHz segment.
notes.example: Like a side road meeting a main road: you give way to the other traffic and put up with its noise.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.303(b) Frequency sharing requirements
notes.evidence: Amateur stations transmitting in the 70 cm band, the 33 cm band, the 23 cm band, the 5 cm band, the 3 cm band, or the 24.05-24.25 GHz segment must not cause harmful interference to, and must accept interference from, stations authorized by the United States Government in the radiolocation service.

notes.front: What is the National Radio Quiet Zone?
notes.back: An area of Maryland, Virginia and West Virginia bounded by 39°15′ N, 78°30′ W, 37°30′ N and 80°30′ W.
notes.explanation: Part 97 defines it by lines of latitude and longitude on a map, not by a distance from any one site.
notes.example: Like a hospital’s no-mobile-phones zone, but drawn as a box on a map across three states.
notes.evidence: The area in Maryland, Virginia and West Virginia Bounded by 39°15′ N on the north, 78°30′ W on the east, 37°30′ N on the south and 80°30′ W on the west.

notes.front: Under 97.15(b), what is reasonable accommodation of amateur antennas?
notes.back: State and local antenna rules must not preclude amateur communications; they must reasonably accommodate them with the minimum practicable regulation.
notes.explanation: The rule cites PRB-1, 101 FCC 2d 952 (1985), for the details.
notes.example: Like a planning rule that may limit how a mast is built but may not ban masts altogether.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.15(b) Station antenna structures
notes.evidence: State and local regulation of a station antenna structure must not preclude amateur service communications. Rather, it must reasonably accommodate such communications and must constitute the minimum practicable regulation to accomplish the state or local authority's legitimate purpose. See PRB-1, 101 FCC 2d 952 (1985) for details.

notes.front: What are the quiet hours of 97.121(a)?
notes.back: No operation from 8 p.m. to 10:30 p.m. local time, and on Sundays also from 10:30 a.m. to 1 p.m., on the offending frequencies.
notes.explanation: The ban covers only the frequency or frequencies in use when the interference is caused, not the whole station.
notes.example: Like a noise curfew on one loud machine in a workshop, while the other machines keep running.
notes.evidence: the amateur station shall not be operated during the hours from 8 p.m. to 10:30 p.m., local time, and on Sunday for the additional period from 10:30 a.m. until 1 p.m., local time, upon the frequency or frequencies used when the interference is created.

notes.front: In RACES, what does a civil defense organization do for a station?
notes.back: It certifies the station as registered with it; without that certificate no station may transmit in RACES.
notes.explanation: The station must also be an FCC-licensed primary, club or military recreation station.
notes.example: Like a volunteer lifeboat crew’s roster: only boats and people on it go out on its call-outs.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.407(a) Radio amateur civil emergency service
notes.evidence: No station may transmit in RACES unless it is an FCC-licensed primary, club, or military recreation station and it is certified by a civil defense organization as registered with that organization.

notes.front: What is telecommand?
notes.back: A one-way transmission to initiate, modify or terminate functions of a device at a distance.
notes.explanation: It is one-way, like telemetry, but carries commands to a device rather than measurements from an instrument.
notes.example: Like a garage-door remote: one-way signals that open, stop or close something out of reach.
notes.evidence: Telecommand. A one-way transmission to initiate, modify, or terminate functions of a device at a distance. (45) Telecommand station. An amateur station that transmits communications to initiate, modify or terminate functions of a space station. (46) Telemetry. A one-way transmission of measurements at a distance from the measuring instrument.

notes.front: What does a space telecommand station do?
notes.back: It transmits communications to start, change or stop the functions of a space station.
notes.explanation: Part 97’s definitions call it a telecommand station: the sender of commands to a space station.
notes.example: Like mission control switching a satellite’s transponder on, but run by an amateur station.
notes.evidence: Telecommand station. An amateur station that transmits communications to initiate, modify or terminate functions of a space station.

notes.front: What is an Earth station?
notes.back: An amateur station on or within 50 km of the Earth’s surface, for communications with space stations, or with Earth stations via objects in space.
notes.explanation: Part 97 defines it by where it is and by what it communicates with.
notes.example: Like a home satellite-television dish, except that it transmits too and talks to amateur satellites.
notes.evidence: An amateur station located on, or within 50 km of, the Earth's surface intended for communications with space stations or with other Earth stations by means of one or more other objects in space.

notes.front: A spurious emission is one whose level may be reduced without affecting the {{c1::information being transmitted}}.
notes.back: information being transmitted
notes.explanation: Part 97 places it outside the necessary bandwidth of the transmission.
notes.evidence: Spurious emission. An emission, or frequencies outside the necessary bandwidth of a transmission, the level of which may be reduced without affecting the information being transmitted.

notes.front: Under 97.307(f)(2), what caps the bandwidth of a non-phone emission such as an image?
notes.back: It must not exceed the bandwidth of a communications-quality phone emission of the same modulation type.
notes.explanation: The limit follows the modulation type: it matches a phone emission of the same kind.
notes.evidence: No non-phone emission shall exceed the bandwidth of a communications quality phone emission of the same modulation type.

notes.front: What may follow if a station within 1600 m of an FCC monitoring facility fails to protect it from harmful interference?
notes.back: Operating restrictions imposed on the amateur station under 97.121.
notes.explanation: Section 97.13(b) sets the 1600 m (1 mile) radius and links the penalty to the restricted-operation rule.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.13(b) Restrictions on station location
notes.evidence: A station within 1600 m (1 mile) of an FCC monitoring facility must protect that facility from harmful interference. Failure to do so could result in imposition of operating restrictions upon the amateur station pursuant to § 97.121.

notes.front: Besides 70 cm, what are two bands where amateurs must accept interference from United States Government radiolocation stations?
notes.back: Any two of: 33 cm, 23 cm, 5 cm, 3 cm (the 24.05–24.25 GHz segment too).
notes.explanation: Section 97.303(b) lists these alongside 70 cm under one sharing rule.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.303(b) Frequency sharing requirements
notes.evidence: Amateur stations transmitting in the 70 cm band, the 33 cm band, the 23 cm band, the 5 cm band, the 3 cm band, or the 24.05-24.25 GHz segment must not cause harmful interference to, and must accept interference from, stations authorized by the United States Government in the radiolocation service.

notes.front: What must a licensee do before setting up an automatically controlled beacon in the National Radio Quiet Zone?
notes.back: Give written notice to the Interference Office of the National Radio Astronomy Observatory at Green Bank, West Virginia.
notes.explanation: The same notice is due before changing the beacon’s frequency, power, antenna height or directivity.
notes.evidence: Before establishing an automatically controlled beacon in the National Radio Quiet Zone or before changing the transmitting frequency, transmitter power, antenna height or directivity, the station licensee must give written notification thereof to the Interference Office, National Radio Astronomy Observatory, P.O. Box 2, Green Bank, WV 24944.

notes.front: Which antenna structures does 97.15(a) require to be notified to the Federal Aviation Administration and registered with the FCC?
notes.back: Certain structures more than 60.96 m (200 ft) above ground, or at or near a public-use airport.
notes.explanation: Registration follows Part 17 of the FCC rules.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.15(a) Station antenna structures
notes.evidence: Owners of certain antenna structures more than 60.96 meters (200 feet) above ground level at the site or located near or at a public use airport must notify the Federal Aviation Administration and register with the Commission as required by part 17 of this chapter.

notes.front: Unless another rule says otherwise, how large may an amateur antenna structure be under 97.15(b)?
notes.back: Of heights and dimensions sufficient to accommodate amateur service communications.
notes.explanation: The test is what amateur service communications need, subject to the section’s other provisions.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.15(b) Station antenna structures
notes.evidence: Except as otherwise provided herein, a station antenna structure may be erected at heights and dimensions sufficient to accommodate amateur service communications.

notes.front: What must be true before the FCC’s quiet hours apply to a station?
notes.back: It causes general interference to domestic broadcast reception on receivers of good engineering design, and the licensee has been told so.
notes.explanation: The rule names receivers of good engineering design, including adequate selectivity.
notes.evidence: If the operation of an amateur station causes general interference to the reception of transmissions from stations operating in the domestic broadcast service when receivers of good engineering design, including adequate selectivity characteristics, are used to receive such transmissions, and this fact is made known to the amateur station licensee,

notes.front: Who may be the control operator of a station transmitting in RACES?
notes.back: A holder of an FCC-issued amateur operator licence who is certified by a civil defense organization as enrolled in it.
notes.explanation: The person needs both an FCC-issued licence and certification as enrolled in the civil defense organization.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.407(a) Radio amateur civil emergency service
notes.evidence: No person may be the control operator of an amateur station transmitting in RACES unless that person holds a FCC-issued amateur operator license and is certified by a civil defense organization as enrolled in that organization.

notes.front: RACES training drills and tests may not exceed a total of {{c1::1 hour}} per week.
notes.back: 1 hour
notes.explanation: With the State’s chief emergency-planning officer’s approval, drills of up to 72 hours may run no more than twice a calendar year.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.407(d)(4) Radio amateur civil emergency service
notes.evidence: Such drills and tests may not exceed a total time of 1 hour per week. With the approval of the chief officer for emergency planning in the applicable State, Commonwealth, District or territory, however, such tests and drills may be conducted for a period not to exceed 72 hours no more than twice in any calendar year.

notes.front: What may space telemetry transmissions consist of, under 97.207(f)?
notes.back: Specially coded messages intended to facilitate communications or related to the function of the spacecraft.
notes.explanation: The codes must facilitate communications or relate to the spacecraft’s function.
notes.evidence: Space telemetry transmissions may consist of specially coded messages intended to facilitate communications or related to the function of the spacecraft.

notes.front: What may a telecommand station send to its space station that ordinary amateur messages may not contain?
notes.back: Special codes intended to obscure the meaning of the telecommand messages.
notes.explanation: Section 97.211(b) allows this for messages to the station in space operation.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.211(b) Space telecommand station
notes.evidence: A telecommand station may transmit special codes intended to obscure the meaning of telecommand messages to the station in space operation.

notes.front: What must every amateur space station be able to do when the FCC orders it?
notes.back: Stop transmitting, on command by telecommand.
notes.explanation: Section 97.207(b) makes this a capability every space station must have.
notes.evidence: A space station must be capable of effecting a cessation of transmissions by telecommand whenever such cessation is ordered by the FCC.

notes.front: Which two kinds of station does 97.119(a) excuse from transmitting their call sign?
notes.back: Space stations and telecommand stations.
notes.explanation: Every other station must send its call sign at the end of each communication and at least every 10 minutes during one.
notes.evidence: Each amateur station, except a space station or telecommand station, must transmit its assigned call sign on its transmitting channel at the end of each communication, and at least every 10 minutes during a communication,

notes.front: How high must an amateur station be for Part 97 to call it a space station?
notes.back: More than 50 km above the Earth’s surface.
notes.explanation: Part 97 defines a space station by its height above the surface alone.
notes.evidence: Space station. An amateur station located more than 50 km above the Earth's surface.

notes.front: A station within 50 km of the Earth’s surface is under telecommand over a radio control link. What must that link use?
notes.back: An auxiliary station.
notes.explanation: A fibre-optic cable or another telecommunication service counts as a wireline link instead.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.213(a) Telecommand of an amateur station
notes.evidence: There is a radio or wireline control link between the control point and the station sufficient for the control operator to perform his/her duties. If radio, the control link must use an auxiliary station. A control link using a fiber optic cable or another telecommunication service is considered wireline.

notes.front: If its control link malfunctions, a telecommanded station must stop transmitting within {{c1::3 minutes}}.
notes.back: 3 minutes
notes.explanation: Section 97.213(b) requires provisions that limit transmission to no more than that period.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.213(b) Telecommand of an amateur station
notes.evidence: Provisions are incorporated to limit transmission by the station to a period of no more than 3 minutes in the event of malfunction in the control link.

notes.front: Which document must be posted, as a photocopy, at a telecommanded station within 50 km of the Earth’s surface?
notes.back: The station licence.
notes.explanation: It must be in a conspicuous place at the station location, beside the contact label.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.213(d) Telecommand of an amateur station
notes.evidence: A photocopy of the station license and a label with the name, address, and telephone number of the station licensee and at least one designated control operator is posted in a conspicuous place at the station location.

notes.front: Whose name, address and telephone number go on the label posted at a telecommanded station?
notes.back: The station licensee’s and at least one designated control operator’s.
notes.explanation: The label is posted with a photocopy of the station licence in a conspicuous place.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.213(d) Telecommand of an amateur station
notes.evidence: A photocopy of the station license and a label with the name, address, and telephone number of the station licensee and at least one designated control operator is posted in a conspicuous place at the station location.

notes.front: When may a transmitter controlling a model craft skip the station identification procedure?
notes.back: For transmissions only to the model craft, if a label with the call sign and licensee’s name and address is on the transmitter.
notes.explanation: The exemption holds only while that label is affixed to the station transmitter.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.215(a) Telecommand of model craft
notes.evidence: The station identification procedure is not required for transmissions directed only to the model craft, provided that a label indicating the station call sign and the station licensee's name and address is affixed to the station transmitter.

notes.front: Which four HF bands are authorised to space stations in full, rather than as a segment?
notes.explanation: On 40 m and 20 m only the 7.0–7.1 MHz and 14.00–14.25 MHz segments are authorised.
notes.evidence: The 17 m, 15 m, 12 m, and 10 m bands, 6 mm, 4 mm, 2 mm and 1 mm bands; and (2) The 7.0-7.1 MHz, 14.00-14.25 MHz, 144-146 MHz, 435-438 MHz,

notes.front: Who may be the control operator of an Earth station?
notes.back: A holder of any class of operator licence, within that class’s privileges.
notes.explanation: Section 97.209(a) also lets any amateur station be an Earth station.
notes.evidence: Any amateur station may be an Earth station. A holder of any class operator license may be the control operator of an Earth station, subject to the privileges of the class of operator license held by the control operator.

notes.front: Your 23 cm station is found to interfere with a United States Government radiolocation station. What does Part 97 require of you?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, because the amateur service is primary on 23 cm
B) Stop causing harmful interference to that station
C) Ask the radiolocation station to accept your interference
D) Move to the 70 cm band, where the rule does not apply
notes.back: Stop causing harmful interference to that station
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule makes amateurs give way here. C: amateurs must accept its interference, not the reverse. D: 70 cm carries the same duty.
notes.explanation: On 23 cm, amateurs must not cause harmful interference to, and must accept interference from, Government radiolocation stations.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.303(b) Frequency sharing requirements
notes.evidence: Amateur stations transmitting in the 70 cm band, the 33 cm band, the 23 cm band, the 5 cm band, the 3 cm band, or the 24.05-24.25 GHz segment must not cause harmful interference to, and must accept interference from, stations authorized by the United States Government in the radiolocation service.

notes.front: Your station is 1.2 km from an FCC monitoring facility. What must you do?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the rule covers only stations within 500 m
B) Protect the facility from harmful interference
C) Operate only during quiet hours
D) Obtain a Special Temporary Authority
notes.back: Protect the facility from harmful interference
notes.choicesExplained: A: the distance in the rule is 1600 m, not 500 m. C: quiet hours are a remedy for broadcast interference, not this rule. D: no authority is needed; the duty is to protect the facility.
notes.explanation: The protection zone is 1600 m (1 mile), so 1.2 km is inside it.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.13(b) Restrictions on station location
notes.evidence: A station within 1600 m (1 mile) of an FCC monitoring facility must protect that facility from harmful interference.

notes.front: You plan a 70 m (about 230 ft) tower far from any airport. What does 97.15(a) mean for you?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, since the rule applies only near airports
B) You may have to notify the Federal Aviation Administration and register the structure with the FCC
C) You must get your neighbours’ written consent
D) You must keep it under 60 m, the limit for all amateur antennas
notes.back: You may have to notify the Federal Aviation Administration and register the structure with the FCC
notes.choicesExplained: A: height alone can bring a structure under the rule. C: 97.15(a) says nothing about neighbours. D: the 60 m cap in 97.15(c) is for 2200 m and 630 m transmitting antennas only.
notes.explanation: Certain structures over 60.96 m (200 ft) need notice to the Federal Aviation Administration and FCC registration under Part 17, airport or not.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.15(a) Station antenna structures
notes.evidence: Owners of certain antenna structures more than 60.96 meters (200 feet) above ground level at the site or located near or at a public use airport must notify the Federal Aviation Administration and register with the Commission as required by part 17 of this chapter.

notes.front: The FCC has told you that your 7.2 MHz signal causes general interference to broadcast reception on good receivers, so the quiet hours apply. Which transmission is still allowed?
notes.choices:
A) 9 p.m. Monday on 7.2 MHz
B) 11 a.m. Sunday on 7.2 MHz
C) 9 p.m. Tuesday on 14.2 MHz
D) 10 p.m. Saturday on 7.2 MHz
notes.back: 9 p.m. Tuesday on 14.2 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: 9 p.m. and 10 p.m. fall inside the daily 8 p.m. to 10:30 p.m. window on the offending frequency. B: 11 a.m. is inside the extra Sunday window, 10:30 a.m. to 1 p.m.
notes.explanation: Quiet hours cover only the frequencies used when the interference is caused.
notes.evidence: the amateur station shall not be operated during the hours from 8 p.m. to 10:30 p.m., local time, and on Sunday for the additional period from 10:30 a.m. until 1 p.m., local time, upon the frequency or frequencies used when the interference is created.

notes.front: An amateur balloon carries a telemetry transmitter to 35 km. Is it a space station?
notes.back: No: a space station must be more than 50 km above the Earth’s surface.
notes.explanation: At 35 km the balloon is below the 50 km line, so it is not a space station.
notes.evidence: Space station. An amateur station located more than 50 km above the Earth's surface.

notes.front: A county civil defence office plans a 3-hour RACES drill every week, with no special approval. Is that allowed?
notes.choices:
A) Yes, RACES drills have no time limit
B) Yes, if every station is certified by the organisation
C) No: drills and tests may total no more than 1 hour a week
D) No: RACES may never hold drills
notes.back: No: drills and tests may total no more than 1 hour a week
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule sets a weekly limit. B: certification lets a station take part but does not lift the time limit. D: drills and tests are one of the permitted RACES communications.
notes.explanation: Longer drills need the State emergency-planning chief’s approval and are limited to 72 hours, twice a calendar year.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.407(d)(4) Radio amateur civil emergency service
notes.evidence: Such drills and tests may not exceed a total time of 1 hour per week. With the approval of the chief officer for emergency planning in the applicable State, Commonwealth, District or territory, however, such tests and drills may be conducted for a period not to exceed 72 hours no more than twice in any calendar year.

notes.front: Telemetry versus telecommand: which way does each carry information?
notes.back: Telemetry: measurements, away from the measuring instrument. Telecommand: commands to a distant device, to start, change or stop its functions.
notes.explanation: Both are one-way transmissions; the difference is what they carry and in which direction.
notes.evidence: Telecommand. A one-way transmission to initiate, modify, or terminate functions of a device at a distance. (45) Telecommand station. An amateur station that transmits communications to initiate, modify or terminate functions of a space station. (46) Telemetry. A one-way transmission of measurements at a distance from the measuring instrument.

notes.front: Messages encoded to obscure their meaning: banned for ordinary amateur traffic, but what exception do telecommand stations have?
notes.back: Ordinary stations may not send them; a telecommand station may send codes that obscure its telecommand messages to a space station.
notes.explanation: The ban on obscured messages applies “except as otherwise provided”, which leaves room for rules such as the telecommand one.
notes.evidence: messages encoded for the purpose of obscuring their meaning, except as otherwise provided herein;

notes.front: One-way communications: what is the general rule, and how do space, beacon and telecommand stations differ?
notes.back: Generally barred unless a rule provides for them; the rules for space, beacon and telecommand stations do provide for them.
notes.explanation: The general rule allows one-way communications only where a rule specifically provides for them.
notes.evidence: nor may an amateur station transmit one-way communications except as specifically provided in these rules;

notes.front: Which of the following constitutes a spurious emission?
notes.choices:
A) An amateur station transmission made without the proper call sign identification
B) A signal transmitted to prevent its detection by any station other than the intended recipient
C) Any transmitted signal that unintentionally interferes with another licensed radio station and whose levels exceed 40 dB below the fundamental power level
D) An emission outside the signal’s necessary bandwidth that can be reduced or eliminated without affecting the information transmitted
notes.back: An emission outside the signal’s necessary bandwidth that can be reduced or eliminated without affecting the information transmitted
notes.choicesExplained: A: a missing call sign is an identification fault, not an emission outside the bandwidth. B: that describes hiding a signal. C: Part 97’s definition has no 40 dB figure and does not depend on interference.
notes.explanation: Part 97 defines a spurious emission as one outside the necessary bandwidth whose level may be reduced without affecting the information sent.
notes.evidence:
D. An emission outside the signal’s necessary bandwidth that can be reduced or eliminated without
affecting the information transmitted

notes.front: Which of the following is an acceptable bandwidth for digital voice or slow-scan TV transmissions made on the HF amateur bands?
notes.choices:
A) 3 kHz
B) 10 kHz
C) 15 kHz
D) 20 kHz
notes.back: 3 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D: 10, 15 and 20 kHz are all wider than the 3 kHz the pool keys for HF digital voice or slow-scan television.
notes.explanation: A communications-quality SSB voice signal is about 3 kHz wide, and 97.307(f)(2) limits a non-phone emission to the width of a phone emission of the same modulation type, so 3 kHz fits.
notes.evidence:
E1B02 (A) [97.307(f)(2)]
Which of the following is an acceptable bandwidth for digital voice or slow-scan TV transmissions made
on the HF amateur bands?
A. 3 kHz
B. 10 kHz
C. 15 kHz
D. 20 kHz

notes.front: Within what distance must an amateur station protect an FCC monitoring facility from harmful interference?
notes.choices:
A) 1 mile
B) 3 miles
C) 10 miles
D) 30 miles
notes.back: 1 mile
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D: 3, 10 and 30 miles are not the distance in 97.13(b).
notes.explanation: Section 97.13(b) sets the radius at 1600 m (1 mile), and a station that fails to protect the facility risks operating restrictions.
notes.evidence:
E1B03 (A) [97.13]
Within what distance must an amateur station protect an FCC monitoring facility from harmful
interference?
A. 1 mile
B. 3 miles
C. 10 miles
D. 30 miles

notes.front: What must the control operator of a repeater operating in the 70-centimeter band do if a radiolocation system experiences interference from that repeater?
notes.choices:
A) Reduce the repeater antenna HAAT (Height Above Average Terrain)
B) File an FAA NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) with the repeater system's ERP, call sign, and six-character grid locator
C) Cease operation or make changes to the repeater that mitigate the interference
D) All these choices are correct
notes.back: Cease operation or make changes to the repeater that mitigate the interference
notes.choicesExplained: A: lowering the antenna is not the duty the rule states; the duty is to end the interference. B: a notice to air missions has nothing to do with this sharing rule. D: A and B are not required, so not all are correct.
notes.explanation: On 70 cm, amateurs must not cause harmful interference to Government radiolocation stations (97.303(b)), so a repeater found interfering must stop, or change until the interference ends.
notes.evidence: C. Cease operation or make changes to the repeater that mitigate the interference

notes.front: What is the National Radio Quiet Zone?
notes.choices:
A) An area surrounding the FCC monitoring station in Laurel, Maryland
B) An area in New Mexico surrounding the White Sands Test Area
C) An area surrounding the National Radio Astronomy Observatory
D) An area in Florida surrounding Cape Canaveral
notes.back: An area surrounding the National Radio Astronomy Observatory
notes.choicesExplained: A: the zone is tied to the radio astronomy observatory, not to an FCC monitoring station. B and D: New Mexico and Florida lie outside the three states that Part 97 names.
notes.explanation: Part 97 defines the zone as an area of Maryland, Virginia and West Virginia; its beacon rule sends notices to the National Radio Astronomy Observatory at Green Bank, West Virginia.
notes.evidence: C. An area surrounding the National Radio Astronomy Observatory

notes.front: Which of the following additional rules apply if you are erecting an amateur station antenna structure at a site at or near a public use airport?
notes.choices:
A) You may have to notify the Federal Aviation Administration and register it with the FCC as required by Part 17 of the FCC rules
B) You may have to enter the height above ground in meters, and the latitude and longitude in degrees, minutes, and seconds on the FAA website
C) You must file an Environmental Impact Statement with the EPA before construction begins
D) You must obtain a construction permit from the airport zoning authority per Part 119 of the FAA regulations
notes.back: You may have to notify the Federal Aviation Administration and register it with the FCC as required by Part 17 of the FCC rules
notes.choicesExplained: B: 97.15(a) does not prescribe entries on any website. C: it says nothing of an environmental impact statement. D: it points to aviation notice and Part 17 registration, not an airport construction permit.
notes.explanation: Section 97.15(a) names structures at or near a public-use airport, as well as certain tall ones, for notice to the Federal Aviation Administration and FCC registration under Part 17.
notes.evidence:
A. You may have to notify the Federal Aviation Administration and register it with the FCC as required by
Part 17 of the FCC rules

notes.front: To what type of regulations does PRB-1 apply?
notes.choices:
A) Homeowners associations
B) FAA tower height limits
C) State and local zoning
D) Use of wireless devices in vehicles
notes.back: State and local zoning
notes.choicesExplained: A: 97.15(b) speaks of state and local regulation; homeowners’ associations are not named. B: Notice for tall structures is 97.15(a), a separate rule. D: vehicle wireless rules are unrelated.
notes.explanation: Section 97.15(b) cites PRB-1 on state and local regulation of antenna structures, which must reasonably accommodate amateur communications.
notes.evidence:
E1B07 (C) [97.15]
To what type of regulations does PRB-1 apply?
A. Homeowners associations
B. FAA tower height limits
C. State and local zoning
D. Use of wireless devices in vehicles

notes.front: What limitations may the FCC place on an amateur station if its signal causes interference to domestic broadcast reception, assuming that the receivers involved are of good engineering design?
notes.choices:
A) The amateur station must cease operation
B) The amateur station must cease operation on all frequencies below 30 MHz
C) The amateur station must cease operation on all frequencies above 30 MHz
D) The amateur station must avoid transmitting during certain hours on frequencies that cause the interference
notes.back: The amateur station must avoid transmitting during certain hours on frequencies that cause the interference
notes.choicesExplained: A: the station is not shut down altogether. B and C: the limit is on the frequencies that cause the interference, not on everything below or above 30 MHz.
notes.explanation: Under 97.121(a) the station must stay off the offending frequencies from 8 p.m. to 10:30 p.m. daily and 10:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Sundays.
notes.evidence:
D. The amateur station must avoid transmitting during certain hours on frequencies that cause the
interference

notes.front: Which amateur stations may be operated under RACES rules?
notes.choices:
A) Only those club stations licensed to Amateur Extra class operators
B) Any FCC-licensed amateur station except a Technician class
C) Any FCC-licensed amateur station certified by the responsible civil defense organization for the area served
D) Only stations meeting the FCC Part 97 technical standards for operation during an emergency
notes.back: Any FCC-licensed amateur station certified by the responsible civil defense organization for the area served
notes.choicesExplained: A: RACES is not limited to club stations or to Extra licensees. B: 97.407 excludes no licence class. D: the test is civil defence certification, not a special technical standard.
notes.explanation: Section 97.407(a) lets an FCC-licensed primary, club or military recreation station transmit in RACES once a civil defense organization certifies it as registered.
notes.evidence:
C. Any FCC-licensed amateur station certified by the responsible civil defense organization for the area
served

notes.front: What frequencies are authorized to an amateur station operating under RACES rules?
notes.choices:
A) All amateur service frequencies authorized to the control operator
B) Specific segments in the amateur service MF, HF, VHF, and UHF bands
C) Specific local government channels
D) All these choices are correct
notes.back: All amateur service frequencies authorized to the control operator
notes.choicesExplained: B: outside a War Emergency Powers emergency, RACES is not confined to special segments. C: local government channels are not amateur frequencies. D: B and C are wrong, so not all are correct.
notes.explanation: RACES stations use the bands, segments and emissions authorised to the control operator, shared with the amateur service (97.407(b)).
notes.evidence: A. All amateur service frequencies authorized to the control operator

notes.front: What does PRB-1 require of state and local regulations affecting amateur radio antenna size and structures?
notes.choices:
A) No limitations may be placed on antenna size or placement
B) Reasonable accommodations of amateur radio must be made
C) Such structures must be permitted when use for emergency communications can be demonstrated
D) Such structures must be permitted if certified by a registered professional engineer
notes.back: Reasonable accommodations of amateur radio must be made
notes.choicesExplained: A: some regulation is allowed, as long as it is the minimum practicable. C and D: the rule asks for reasonable accommodation, not permission tied to emergency use or an engineer’s certificate.
notes.explanation: Section 97.15(b) says such regulation must not preclude amateur communications, but reasonably accommodate them with the minimum practicable regulation.
notes.evidence: B. Reasonable accommodations of amateur radio must be made

notes.front: What is the definition of telemetry?
notes.choices:
A) One-way transmission of measurements at a distance from the measuring instrument
B) Two-way transmissions in excess of 1000 feet
C) Two-way transmissions of data
D) One-way transmission that initiates, modifies, or terminates the functions of a device at a distance
notes.back: One-way transmission of measurements at a distance from the measuring instrument
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: telemetry is one-way, not two-way. D: a one-way transmission that starts, changes or stops a device is telecommand.
notes.explanation: Part 97 defines telemetry as a one-way transmission of measurements at a distance from the measuring instrument.
notes.evidence: A. One-way transmission of measurements at a distance from the measuring instrument

notes.front: Which of the following may transmit encrypted messages?
notes.choices:
A) Telecommand signals to terrestrial repeaters
B) Telecommand signals from a space telecommand station
C) Auxiliary relay links carrying repeater audio
D) Mesh network backbone nodes
notes.back: Telecommand signals from a space telecommand station
notes.choicesExplained: A: the exception covers telecommand to a station in space, not to terrestrial repeaters. C and D: repeater links and mesh nodes fall under the general ban on messages encoded to obscure their meaning.
notes.explanation: Section 97.211(b) lets a telecommand station send special codes that obscure the meaning of its messages to the space station.
notes.evidence: B. Telecommand signals from a space telecommand station

notes.front: What is a space telecommand station?
notes.choices:
A) An amateur station located on the surface of the Earth for communication with other Earth stations by means of Earth satellites
B) An amateur station that transmits communications to initiate, modify, or terminate functions of a space station
C) An amateur station located in a satellite or a balloon more than 50 kilometers above the surface of the Earth
D) An amateur station that receives telemetry from a satellite or balloon more than 50 kilometers above the surface of the Earth
notes.back: An amateur station that transmits communications to initiate, modify, or terminate functions of a space station
notes.choicesExplained: A: a station on the ground working others through satellites is an Earth station. C: a station more than 50 km up is a space station. D: receiving telemetry is not telecommand.
notes.explanation: Part 97 defines a telecommand station by what it sends: communications that start, change or stop a space station’s functions.
notes.evidence:
B. An amateur station that transmits communications to initiate, modify, or terminate functions of a
space station

notes.front: Which of the following is required in the identification transmissions from a balloon-borne telemetry station?
notes.choices:
A) Call sign
B) The output power of the balloon transmitter
C) The station's six-character Maidenhead grid locator
D) All these choices are correct
notes.back: Call sign
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the rule requires the assigned call sign, not the power or a grid locator. D: B and C are not required, so not all are correct.
notes.explanation: Section 97.119(a) excuses only space and telecommand stations from sending their call sign, and a balloon below 50 km is neither.
notes.evidence:
E1D04 (A) [97.119(a)]
Which of the following is required in the identification transmissions from a balloon-borne telemetry
station?
A. Call sign
B. The output power of the balloon transmitter
C. The station's six-character Maidenhead grid locator
D. All these choices are correct

notes.front: What must be posted at the location of a station being operated by telecommand on or within 50 kilometers of the Earth’s surface?
notes.choices:
A) A photocopy of the station license
B) A label with the name, address, and telephone number of the station licensee
C) A label with the name, address, and telephone number of the control operator
D) All these choices are correct
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: each is only one part of what 97.213(d) requires to be posted.
notes.explanation: Section 97.213(d) requires a photocopy of the station licence and a label with the licensee’s and at least one control operator’s name, address and telephone number.
notes.evidence:
E1D05 (D) [97.213(d)]
What must be posted at the location of a station being operated by telecommand on or within 50
kilometers of the Earth’s surface?
A. A photocopy of the station license
B. A label with the name, address, and telephone number of the station licensee

notes.front: What is the maximum permitted transmitter output power when operating a model craft by telecommand?
notes.choices:
A) 1 watt
B) 2 watts
C) 5 watts
D) 100 watts
notes.back: 1 watt
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D: 2, 5 and 100 W all exceed the 1 W cap.
notes.explanation: Section 97.215(c) says the transmitter power must not exceed 1 W.
notes.evidence:
What is the maximum permitted transmitter output power when operating a model craft by
telecommand?
A. 1 watt
B. 2 watts
C. 5 watts
D. 100 watts

notes.front: Which of the following HF amateur bands include allocations for space stations?
notes.choices:
A) 40 meters, 20 meters, 15 meters, and 10 meters
B) 30 meters, 17 meters, and 10 meters
C) Only 10 meters
D) Satellite operation is permitted on all HF bands
notes.back: 40 meters, 20 meters, 15 meters, and 10 meters
notes.choicesExplained: B: 97.207(c) lists nothing on 30 m. C: 10 m is not the only one. D: space stations are not authorised on every HF band.
notes.explanation: Section 97.207(c) authorises 7.0–7.1 MHz, 14.00–14.25 MHz and the whole of 17, 15, 12 and 10 m; the keyed answer names four of these bands.
notes.evidence: A. 40 meters, 20 meters, 15 meters, and 10 meters

notes.front: Which VHF amateur bands have frequencies authorized for space stations?
notes.choices:
A) 6 meters and 2 meters
B) 6 meters, 2 meters, and 1.25 meters
C) 2 meters and 1.25 meters
D) 2 meters
notes.back: 2 meters
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: 97.207(c) lists no 6 m or 1.25 m segment for space stations.
notes.explanation: Section 97.207(c) authorises 144–146 MHz, in the 2 m band, to space stations.
notes.evidence:

A. 6 meters and 2 meters
B. 6 meters, 2 meters, and 1.25 meters
C. 2 meters and 1.25 meters
D. 2 meters

notes.front: Which UHF amateur bands have frequencies authorized for space stations?
notes.choices:
A) 70 centimeters only
B) 70 centimeters and 13 centimeters
C) 70 centimeters and 33 centimeters
D) 33 centimeters and 13 centimeters
notes.back: 70 centimeters and 13 centimeters
notes.choicesExplained: A: the 13 cm segment is authorised too. C and D: 97.207(c) lists no 33 cm segment for space stations.
notes.explanation: Section 97.207(c) authorises 435–438 MHz and 2400–2450 MHz to space stations; the pool places these in the 70 cm and 13 cm bands.
notes.evidence:
E1D09 (B) [97.207]
Which UHF amateur bands have frequencies authorized for space stations?
A. 70 centimeters only
B. 70 centimeters and 13 centimeters
C. 70 centimeters and 33 centimeters
D. 33 centimeters and 13 centimeters

notes.front: Which amateur stations are eligible to be telecommand stations of space stations, subject to the privileges of the class of operator license held by the control operator of the station?
notes.choices:
A) Any amateur station approved by AMSAT
B) Any amateur station so designated by the space station licensee
C) Any amateur station so designated by the ITU
D) All these choices are correct
notes.back: Any amateur station so designated by the space station licensee
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the choice is the space station licensee’s, not a satellite group’s or an international body’s. D: A and C are wrong, so not all are correct.
notes.explanation: Under 97.211(a), any amateur station designated by the space station’s licensee may be its telecommand station, within the control operator’s privileges.
notes.evidence: B. Any amateur station so designated by the space station licensee

notes.front: Which amateur stations are eligible to operate as Earth stations?
notes.choices:
A) Any amateur licensee who has successfully completed the AMSAT space communications course
B) Only those of General, Advanced or Amateur Extra class operators
C) Only those of Amateur Extra class operators
D) Any amateur station, subject to the privileges of the class of operator license held by the control operator
notes.back: Any amateur station, subject to the privileges of the class of operator license held by the control operator
notes.choicesExplained: A: no course is required. B and C: the rule is open to every licence class, not only the higher ones.
notes.explanation: Section 97.209(a) says any amateur station may be an Earth station, and a holder of any licence class may be its control operator.
notes.evidence:
D. Any amateur station, subject to the privileges of the class of operator license held by the control
operator

notes.front: Which of the following amateur stations may transmit one-way communications?
notes.choices:
A) A space station, beacon station, or telecommand station
B) A local repeater or linked repeater station
C) A message forwarding station or automatically controlled digital station
D) All these choices are correct
notes.back: A space station, beacon station, or telecommand station
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the rules the pool cites give this exception to space stations and beacons, and 97.211(d) to telecommand stations, not to these stations. D: so not all are correct.
notes.explanation: Sections 97.207(e), 97.203(g) and 97.211(d) allow one-way communications for space stations, beacons and telecommand stations respectively.
notes.evidence: A. A space station, beacon station, or telecommand station
